Many models in applied work have likelihoods that depend on the data only through a few summary numbers. When that
holds, you can fit the model to the summaries instead of the rows and get the same posterior. The fit is faster, often
by one or two orders of magnitude, because the sampler no longer touches every row on every step.

This post collects the cases I have found useful. Each case has its own notebook. Every notebook fits the same model
twice, once on the raw rows and once on the summary, checks that the posteriors agree, and times both fits. The figures
and tables below are taken from those notebooks.

## Why sufficiency saves computation

Suppose the likelihood factors as

$$p(y \mid \theta) = h(y)\, g\big(T(y) \mid \theta\big).$$

The factor $h(y)$ does not depend on $\theta$, so it cancels in Bayes' rule. The posterior is then
$p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(\theta)\, g(T(y) \mid \theta)$, and it depends on the data only through $T(y)$. This is the
Fisher–Neyman factorisation. A statistic $T$ with this property is called **sufficient**.

The computational gain comes from how Hamiltonian Monte Carlo works. Each leapfrog step evaluates the log-likelihood and
its gradient. A likelihood written over $N$ rows costs $N$ row evaluations per step, and a fit takes thousands of steps
per chain. A likelihood written over $T(y)$ costs only as much as $T(y)$ is large.

Exponential families always have such a statistic. Their densities take the form
$h(y)\exp\{\eta(\theta)^\top T(y) - A(\theta)\}$, and the sum of $T$ over independent observations is sufficient,
with a dimension that does not grow with $n$. The Pitman–Koopman–Darmois theorem gives the converse. If the support of
the distribution does not depend on $\theta$, only exponential families have a sufficient statistic of fixed dimension.
Binomial, Poisson, Normal and multinomial models qualify. Student-$t$ errors and mixtures do not.

For computation, sufficiency for $y$ is not quite enough. In a logistic regression the outcome enters the
log-likelihood only through $X^\top y$, so $X^\top y$ is sufficient for the coefficients. But the log-likelihood also
contains the term $\sum_i \log(1 + e^{x_i^\top\beta})$, which needs every row's covariates. What we need is a
fixed-size summary of the whole likelihood as a function of the parameters. There are two common ways to get one:

1. **Shared covariates.** If rows fall into cells with identical covariates, the likelihood depends on each cell only
   through a few counts. The Binomial, Poisson and multinomial cases below work this way.
2. **A quadratic log-likelihood.** In the Gaussian linear model the log-likelihood is quadratic in the coefficients, so
   the covariates enter only through cross-products. The linear regression case works this way.

The last case in the catalogue fits neither pattern. There the summary is an approximation.

## What compression gives up

The posterior is unchanged, but the individual rows are gone. Any check that needs the rows is no longer possible.
If user-level conversions become $(n, k)$, you cannot check whether conversions cluster within users. If revenue
becomes $(n, \bar y, SS)$, you cannot see a large share of zero-revenue users that a Normal model ignores. Run these
checks on the raw data, or on a sample of it, before you compress.

The covariates decide how much compression is possible. Each categorical covariate multiplies the number of cells.
A continuous covariate usually gives each row its own cell, which removes the gain. Linear regression is the exception,
for the algebraic reason above. A random effect at the row level, such as a user's frailty, makes rows in the same cell
no longer interchangeable, so the counts stop being sufficient.

## A/B tests: counts and moments

In a conversion test each user is a Bernoulli trial. The likelihood for an arm is $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, so the number of
users $n$ and the number of conversions $k$ are sufficient. A `pm.Binomial` on two rows replaces a `pm.Bernoulli` on
800,000.

For a continuous outcome under a Normal model, the count, mean and sum of squared deviations $(n, \bar y, SS)$ are
sufficient for $(\mu, \sigma)$. The notebook writes the exact Normal log-likelihood in terms of these three numbers and
adds it with `pm.Potential`. A `Potential` adds a term to the model's log-density without declaring an observed
variable.

The left panel below also shows the exact Beta posterior, which conjugacy gives without sampling. All three posteriors
for the conversion lift agree.

## Sequential tests: running counts

Checking a fixed-sample test repeatedly as data arrive inflates its false-positive rate. Lindon and Malek,
*Anytime-Valid Inference for Multinomial Count Data* (NeurIPS 2022), give a test that can be checked after every event
while keeping the type-I error below the nominal level. Such a test is called anytime-valid. Their test statistic is a
Dirichlet–multinomial Bayes factor. By their Eq. 3, it depends on the event stream only through $\mathbf S_n$, the
running count of events in each arm.

This has two practical consequences. First, updating the test after an event means adding one to one count. Second, a
shared time-varying baseline does not need to be modelled. Suppose each arm's events arrive as a Poisson process with
rate equal to an arm-specific multiplier times a common baseline $\lambda(t)$. Given that an event occurred, the arm it
came from is a multinomial draw whose probabilities do not involve $\lambda(t)$. In the simulation the baseline has a
daily cycle and a two-day promotion, and the test ignores both.

{{< embed notebooks/02_sequential_multinomial.ipynb#fig-seq-path >}}

Because the statistic depends only on running counts, its error rate is cheap to check by simulation. In 1,000
simulated A/A tests, where all arms are identical, the anytime-valid test checked after every event rejected 3.8% of
the time. A chi-square test re-run every 250 events rejected 31% of the time. For estimation, one `pm.Multinomial` on
the final counts gives the same posterior as the event-level model and the conjugate Dirichlet.

## Survival: events and exposure

A discrete-time survival model is fitted to a person-period table. It has one row for each subject in each period they
are at risk, with a 0/1 flag for the event. With categorical covariates, all rows in a cell defined by period and
covariate pattern share one hazard. The cell then reduces to its number of events and number at risk, $(d, r)$. This is
the life table. The notebook uses the complementary log-log link, $h = 1 - \exp(-e^{\eta})$, which makes the discrete
model a grouped form of a proportional-hazards model.

The continuous-time version is the piecewise-exponential model. Each subject contributes their time at risk in each
interval, and each cell reduces to its events and total exposure, $(d, E)$. Its likelihood is proportional to a Poisson
likelihood with a log-exposure offset. That is why Poisson regression with an exposure offset can be used as a survival
model. I used the same aggregation in the
[discrete-time survival notebook for Bambi](https://nathanielf.github.io/oss/bambi/survival_discrete_time_notebook.html)
on historical child-mortality data.

The cloglog and piecewise-exponential models are different models, so they need not agree with each other. Each
compressed fit agrees with its own raw-row fit.

## Markov chains and funnels: transition counts

A user session is a sequence of states, such as landing page, product page, cart, checkout, then purchase or exit. In a
first-order Markov chain the next state depends only on the current one. The likelihood of a set of sessions is then
$\prod_{ij} P_{ij}^{N_{ij}}$, where $N_{ij}$ counts the transitions from state $i$ to state $j$. The count matrix is
sufficient. Each row of the transition matrix gets a multinomial likelihood and a Dirichlet prior.

The quantity of interest is often the probability that a session starting on the landing page ends in a purchase. Split
the transition matrix into moves between transient states, $Q$, and moves into the absorbing states, $R$. The absorption
probabilities are $B = (I - Q)^{-1} R$. The notebook computes $B$ as a deterministic, so its posterior reflects the
uncertainty in every transition.

A funnel is a special case in which a user can only advance one stage or leave. Each stage then becomes a binomial on
head-counts: the number who reached stage $k+1$ out of the number who reached stage $k$. The notebook lets step
conversion vary by weekly cohort with a hierarchical prior. The compressed model has 36 rows.

## Linear regression: the Gram matrix

The Gaussian linear model compresses without grouping rows. Expand the residual sum of squares:

$$\lVert y - X\beta\rVert^2 = y^\top y - 2\beta^\top X^\top y + \beta^\top X^\top X\beta.$$

The likelihood for $(\beta, \sigma)$ needs only $n$, $X^\top X$, $X^\top y$ and $y^\top y$. $X^\top X$ is the Gram
matrix of cross-products between predictors. The predictors can be continuous. In the notebook, one million rows and ten
predictors reduce to 112 numbers.

These summaries add across subsets of the data. You can compute them on separate chunks, partitions or days and sum
the results. The notebook builds them in ten chunks.

## Approximate sufficiency: logistic regression with offsets

The [football factor model](https://nathanielf.github.io/football_models_with_wyatt/) I built with Wyatt includes a
logistic regression with a per-shot offset. Each shot has a pre-shot goal probability $p_i$ from an expected-goals
model. A player's finishing skill $\eta$ shifts the log-odds of every shot they take. Goals $G = \sum_i y_i$ are
sufficient for $\eta$, but the normalising term sums over every shot's offset, so neither exact route applies.

A second-order expansion of the log-likelihood around $\eta = 0$ gives

$$\ell(\eta) \approx \ell(0) + (G - X)\,\eta - \tfrac12 V \eta^2,$$

with $X = \sum_i p_i$ (expected goals) and $V = \sum_i p_i(1 - p_i)$. Three numbers per player replace the shots.
Completing the square gives a Gaussian pseudo-observation, $(G - X)/V \sim \mathcal N(\eta, 1/\sqrt V)$. This is the
same form as the eight-schools meta-analysis, where each unit contributes an estimate and a standard error. It can be
fitted with an ordinary `pm.Normal`.

The figure shows the exact and approximate log-likelihood for one player. They agree closely within about 0.3 log-odds
units of zero, which covers plausible finishing effects.

{{< embed notebooks/06_approximate_sufficiency.ipynb#fig-approx-curve >}}

The notebook also tests a case where skill varies far more than is realistic. Expanded around zero, the approximation
overstates the skill of the most extreme players. Expanding each player around a one-step estimate of their own skill
removes the error. This requires one more pass over the shots.

## Timings

| Model family | Raw rows | Sufficient statistic | PyMC likelihood | Speed-up in notebook |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conversion test | Bernoulli per user | $(n, k)$ per arm | `Binomial` | 38× (46s → 1.2s) |
| Normal outcome | value per user | $(n, \bar y, SS)$ per arm | `Potential` | 10× (11s → 1.1s) |
| Sequential multinomial | arm label per event | running counts $\mathbf S_n$ | `Multinomial` / closed form | 3× (6.4s → 2.2s) |
| Discrete-time survival | person-period rows | $(d, r)$ per cell | `Binomial` (cloglog) | 51× (87s → 1.7s) |
| Piecewise exponential | person-interval rows | $(d, E)$ per cell | `Poisson` with exposure | 20× (35s → 1.7s) |
| Markov chain | transitions | counts $N_{ij}$ | `Multinomial` per row | 24× (186s → 7.9s) |
| Funnel | user × stage rows | stage head-counts | `Binomial` | 12× (13s → 1.1s) |
| Linear regression | $n \times p$ design | $(n, X^\top X, X^\top y, y^\top y)$ | `Potential` | 76× (189s → 2.5s) |
| Logistic with offsets | shots | $(G, X, V)$, approximate | `Normal` pseudo-obs | 57× (80s → 1.4s) |

Each speed-up is the wall time of the raw-row fit divided by the wall time of the compressed fit. Both include
compilation, and both use the same sampler settings on a laptop. The ratios depend on how many rows each notebook
simulates. The general point is that computing the summaries takes one pass over the data, and after that the cost of
sampling does not depend on the number of rows.

## Practical notes

Run row-level posterior predictive checks before compressing. Compression removes the rows those checks need. You can
keep a raw-data model, fitted to a sample, for diagnostics.

Use an observed distribution rather than `pm.Potential` when one exists. `Binomial`, `Multinomial`, `Poisson` and the
Gaussian pseudo-observation all keep a pointwise log-likelihood, so leave-one-out cross-validation still works. It now
works at the level of the cell rather than the individual.

Counts, exposures and Gram matrices are additive. They can be summed across days, partitions or machines. This makes
them well suited to streaming data and to data held in a warehouse, where the summaries can be computed in SQL.

Approximate summaries depend on their expansion point. They are accurate near that point and less accurate far from it.
Summaries computed around different expansion points cannot be added together.

Each summary also states an assumption of the model. Writing down $(n, k)$ says which users are interchangeable.
Writing down $(d, r)$ says which covariates define a risk set. Writing down $N_{ij}$ says that the next step depends only
on the current state. If one of those statements is false for your data, the compressed model is wrong in the same way
the full model is, and it is cheaper to find out by checking the statement directly.

The notebooks are in the [project folder](https://github.com/NathanielF/NathanielF.github.io/tree/master/posts/post-with-code/SufficientStatistics).
I plan to add more cases.
